Non-Compete.summary: Restricts your ability to work for competitors after the contract ends.
Non-Compete.why_risky: Non-competes can kill your career options. If you sign one, you may be unable to take another job in your field for 1-2 years, even if this employer lays you off.
Non-Compete.real_example: A software engineer signs a 2-year non-compete with TechCo. Six months later, TechCo goes bankrupt. The engineer wants to join Google (obviously a competitor), but can't without risking a lawsuit. She has to change careers or move to a country where the clause doesn't apply.
red_flags: Duration: How long? (1 year is harsh; 6 months is reasonable)
Geography: Worldwide or just your city? (Worldwide is extreme)
Industry scope: Does it block all tech jobs, or only TechCo's exact product?
what_to_negotiate: Reduce duration from 2 years to 6 months
Limit to your current city or country, not worldwide
Narrow 'competitor' to only direct competitors, not all tech companies
Add: 'Void if employer terminates without cause'

Exclusivity.summary: You must work only for this company; no side projects, freelancing, or other jobs.
Exclusivity.why_risky: Exclusivity clauses can trap you. You can't earn extra income, start a side business, or even volunteer if it competes with the company's interests.
Exclusivity.real_example: A freelancer signs an exclusive contract for 6 months. During that time, a friend offers a lucrative 1-week gig for a different client. The freelancer must refuse or risk being sued for breach. Six months of zero side income while living paycheck-to-paycheck.
red_flags: Does 'work' include unpaid activities like volunteering?
Does it block ALL side income or only competing work?
Is the exclusivity period reasonable (full-time vs. part-time)?
what_to_negotiate: Limit to direct competitors only, allow unrelated side work
Add hourly/part-time carve-out: 'May do up to 10 hours/week of unrelated work'
Add: 'Does not apply to investments or passive income'

Uncapped Liability.summary: You are responsible for ANY losses caused by your work, with no upper limit.
Uncapped Liability.why_risky: One mistake could bankrupt you. If you're a freelancer or small business owner, unlimited liability exposure is catastrophic. A single bug, missed deadline, or miscommunication could result in a lawsuit for 10x what you earned.
Uncapped Liability.real_example: A freelance web developer builds a website for an e-commerce startup. A security flaw lets hackers steal customer credit cards. The startup sues for $500,000 in damages and lost business. The developer's contract has no liability cap, so she's personally liable for the full amount. Her insurance doesn't cover it because she breached a contract term. She declares bankruptcy.
red_flags: The phrase 'shall be liable for all losses' or 'unlimited liability'
No mention of a cap or ceiling
Liability includes 'consequential damages' (indirect, long-term losses)
what_to_negotiate: Add a cap: 'Liability capped at fees paid in the past 12 months' (so max 1 year of income at risk)
Exclude 'consequential damages': 'Neither party liable for lost profits or business interruption'
Add: 'Liability only for direct, foreseeable losses'
Get errors & omissions insurance and mention it in the contract

Liquidated Damages.summary: You owe a fixed payment if you miss a deadline or fail to perform.
Liquidated Damages.why_risky: Liquidated damages clauses can be unreasonable traps. They often penalize you for delays even if the delay wasn't your fault (e.g., client was slow to provide feedback). The fixed amount may be far higher than the client's actual loss.
Liquidated Damages.real_example: A contractor agrees to deliver a website on 1 Jan, with liquidated damages of $5,000/day for delay. The client delays approving designs by 2 weeks. The contractor finally finishes on 1 Mar. The contract says delays are still liable to damages, even though the delay was the client's fault. The contractor owes $30,000.
red_flags: A specific dollar amount or percentage mentioned as a penalty
No exemption for delays caused by the client
No upper limit on total damages
what_to_negotiate: Ensure damages are a 'genuine pre-estimate of loss', not a penalty. Ask: 'How did you calculate this number?'
Add: 'Liquidated damages only apply if the delay is solely caused by Contractor'
Add carve-out: 'Client delays, change orders, and acts beyond Contractor's control are excluded'
Cap total damages: 'Total LD shall not exceed 10% of contract value'
Require written notice before damages accrue

Termination for Convenience.summary: Either party can end the contract at any time, for any reason, by giving notice.
Termination for Convenience.why_risky: This is one-sided if only the employer can use it. You could lose your job with 2 weeks' notice while you're contractually locked in. If it's mutual, it's fair.
Termination for Convenience.real_example: An employee signs a contract that says 'Company may terminate at any time with 48 hours' notice.' Six months later, after the employee turns down a promotion (upset the wrong manager), she's fired with 2 days' notice and no severance. The employee had assumed she had job security; she didn't.
red_flags: Only the employer/client can terminate for convenience; employee/contractor cannot
Very short notice period (< 2 weeks)
No severance or payment for unused notice
what_to_negotiate: Make it mutual: 'Either party may terminate for convenience'
Extend notice to 30 days (minimum)
Add severance: 'Two weeks' pay + unused vacation' or 'One month's salary if terminated in first year'
Add: 'Termination for convenience does not apply during the first 6 months'

Anti-Assignment.summary: You cannot transfer the contract to another person or company; the other party can.
Anti-Assignment.why_risky: This is a trap if it's one-sided. You can't sell your freelance business or pass work to a subcontractor, but the client can sell your contract to a larger competitor with no consent.
Anti-Assignment.real_example: A small agency signs a contract saying 'Agency may not assign this work to other vendors without Client approval.' One year later, the Client sells its business to a huge multinational. The contract is automatically assigned to the new owner. The agency is now working for a company it didn't choose, on terms set by someone else.
red_flags: Only one party is restricted from assigning
Client/employer can assign freely; you cannot assign at all
No mention of consent requirements for either side
what_to_negotiate: Make it mutual: 'Neither party may assign without the other's written consent (not to be unreasonably withheld)'
Add exception: 'Client may assign to buyers in M&A transactions with 30 days' notice; Contractor may assign to subcontractors of equivalent capability with written notice'
Add: 'If assigned to a competitor or entity using different labor practices, Contractor may terminate without penalty'

Cap on Liability.summary: Your liability is capped at a specific amount (often the fees you earned).
Cap on Liability.why_risky: This is actually GOOD for you if you're the liable party. It protects you from catastrophic losses. (It's bad if the other party wants to cap YOUR liability while their liability is unlimited.)
Cap on Liability.real_example: A freelancer's contract says 'Contractor's liability capped at fees paid in the past 12 months.' A coding error causes the client to lose $100,000. Because of the cap, the freelancer only owes $30,000 (last year's fees), not $100,000. The cap saved her from financial ruin.
red_flags: Cap is higher than expected (e.g., '2x annual fees' is high; '1x annual fees' is standard)
Liability cap is mutual: both parties have limits (good). Liability cap is one-sided: only you are capped, they are not (bad)
what_to_negotiate: If the cap is too high, negotiate down to 1x fees or 1x contract value
Ensure it's mutual: 'Both parties' liability capped at...'
Add exception: 'Cap does not apply to indemnification, IP infringement, or confidentiality breaches'

Audit Rights.summary: The other party can inspect your books, records, or work to verify compliance.
Audit Rights.why_risky: Audit rights are low-risk if they're reasonable (notice required, once per year, at their cost). They're risky if they're vague ("anytime, for any reason, and you pay").
Audit Rights.real_example: A vendor contract says 'Client may audit Vendor's records once per year on 30 days' notice.' The vendor can plan for the audit and prepare records. Once per year is reasonable and predictable.
red_flags: No notice period required; audits can happen anytime, without warning
Unlimited frequency: 'Client may audit at any time'
You have to pay for the audit, even if it finds nothing wrong
what_to_negotiate: Require written notice: 'At least 30 days before audit'
Limit frequency: 'Once per calendar year, unless previous audit found discrepancies'
Cost allocation: 'Auditor costs borne by Client; if discrepancy > 5%, Contractor reimburses audit cost'
Add confidentiality: 'Auditor bound by NDA'

Change of Control.summary: If the company is sold, acquired, or merged, the contract may be terminated or renegotiated.
Change of Control.why_risky: You have no say in whether your contract survives a merger. A new owner might terminate your contract, change terms, or move your work to a different vendor.
Change of Control.real_example: An employee works at StartupX for 3 years with a generous benefits package. StartupX is acquired by BigCorp. BigCorp invokes the 'Change of Control' clause and terminates all StartupX employees without severance, replacing them with BigCorp's staff. The employee has no recourse.
red_flags: Contract automatically terminates on acquisition (no choice for you)
New owner can unilaterally change terms
No severance or notification period if terminated due to change of control
what_to_negotiate: Add: 'Change of Control does not automatically terminate this contract'
Add: 'If terminated due to Change of Control, Contractor entitled to 6 weeks severance'
Add: 'New owner must assume all existing terms or give 90 days notice and severance'
Add: 'Contractor may terminate without penalty if new owner is a direct competitor'

IP Ownership Assignment.summary: You assign all intellectual property (code, designs, ideas) you create to the client/employer.
IP Ownership Assignment.why_risky: If you work on something innovative, you lose all rights to it. You can't reuse the code, the design, or even the concepts in future projects (because they might infringe the client's IP).
IP Ownership Assignment.real_example: A developer creates a novel caching algorithm for a client's e-commerce site. The algorithm is brilliant and could be reused in many projects. But the contract assigns all IP to the client. The developer can never use it again, even for unrelated clients. Years later, the developer rebuilds the same algorithm from scratch for a different client, wasting weeks.
red_flags: You assign ALL inventions, even unrelated ones created outside work hours
No carve-out for pre-existing tools, libraries, or methodologies you owned before
No carve-out for work created on your own time with your own resources
what_to_negotiate: Narrow scope: 'IP ownership limited to work-product directly related to Services'
Add: 'Developer retains ownership of pre-existing tools, libraries, and methodologies'
Add: 'Developer may reuse general techniques and knowledge gained, but not specific code/designs'
Add: 'Developer may use anonymized examples for portfolio/learning (NDA-protected)'
Compromise: 'Client owns IP; Developer retains perpetual, royalty-free license to reuse for non-competitive purposes'

No Clause.summary: This clause does not fall into a risky category. It's standard boilerplate.
No Clause.why_risky: Not risky. This is normal contract language (definitions, governing law, confidentiality, etc.).
No Clause.real_example: A contract says 'This Agreement is governed by the laws of California.' This is a jurisdiction clause, not a risky clause. It just determines which court handles disputes.
